title: When the Portrait Wakes
premise: Juniper Zhou returns to Hollowmere to bury her twin sister Wren, only to discover the body in the coffin is not Wren — and that the village's melted church bell has begun ringing at dusk, calling the living to finish a hymn whose last verse was never sung. The bell is a trap left by villagers who, in 1911, drowned a wrongfully accused woman and silenced the song that could have freed her; whoever completes the verse becomes her voice, and whoever refuses becomes her replacement. Juniper learns Wren discovered the truth and tried to sing the verse alone, paying with her life. In the end, Juniper sings the final verse not as the ghost's mouth but as a witness naming the guilty dead, shattering the bell's hold — though she leaves Hollowmere knowing justice bought with a sister's grave is a debt she will carry forever.
about_author: Yara Dunmore is the pen name of a former parish archivist from coastal Maine who spent years cataloguing drowned-town records before turning to horror. Her fiction draws on hymnals, flood ledgers, and the stubborn arithmetic of small-town guilt.

chapters.title: The Wrong Face in the Coffin
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Arriving for the funeral, she lifts the coffin lid and finds a stranger wearing Wren's ring, while the funeral home insists no other body was delivered. The village closes ranks with practiced smiles. Emotional beat: grief curdling into dread as loyalty to her sister demands an answer no one will give.

chapters.title: A Bell That Was Never Cast
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, with fragments of Wren's journal. At dusk the melted bell rings, and every villager freezes mid-motion, lips moving on a verse they refuse to finish. Wren's journal reveals the 1911 drowning and warns: learn the last verse, never sing it. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as the town's kindness reveals itself as containment.

chapters.title: The Verse Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Following Wren's clues to the flooded chapel ruins, she recovers the hidden verse and the drowned woman's name, but the bell begins ringing at noon too, and neighbors start sleepwalking toward her door, singing everything but the end. Emotional beat: terror of complicity — the song wants her voice, and part of her wants to give it.

chapters.title: Sung by a Witness
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. On the centenary night the bell rings without stopping; the village gathers to force her to sing and take Wren's place. Instead she speaks the verse aloud, naming the 1911 killers and their descendants, refusing melody for testimony. The bell cracks; the ghost releases Wren's true body from the water. Emotional beat: costly resolution — truth served, survival paid for in permanent exile from peace.
